items.text: “Take a focused history from a woman presenting with chronic pelvic pain.”
“A 29-year-old woman has had pelvic pain for eight months. Take a history, discuss your differential diagnoses and outline your management.”
“Examine a patient with chronic pelvic pain and present your findings.”
“Counsel a woman with suspected endometriosis presenting with chronic pelvic pain.”
“Discuss the investigations and management of chronic pelvic pain.”

blocks.text: Your priorities are to identify the cause where possible, assess the effect on daily life and fertility, and exclude urgent or serious pathology.

Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is persistent or recurrent pain perceived in the pelvis, usually lasting at least six months in traditional clinical definitions, although some modern definitions do not require a fixed duration. It may be cyclical or non-cyclical and may occur with menstruation, sexual intercourse, urination, defecation or physical activity.
Gynaecological causes

items.text: Endometriosis
Adenomyosis
Uterine fibroids
Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and adhesions
Ovarian cysts or other adnexal pathology
Pelvic congestion syndrome
Pelvic floor dysfunction

blocks.text: Urinary causes

items.text: Bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis
Recurrent urinary tract infection
Urolithiasis
Other bladder or ureteric disorders

blocks.text: Gastrointestinal causes

items.text: Irritable bowel syndrome
Constipation
Inflammatory bowel disease
Diverticular disease, where relevant
Chronic appendiceal or other abdominal pathology

blocks.text: Musculoskeletal and other causes

items.text: Pelvic floor muscle tenderness or spasm
Abdominal wall pain
Sacroiliac or hip pathology
Neuropathic pain
Pain associated with previous surgery or trauma
Psychological distress that may amplify pain

blocks.text: Important OSCE principle: chronic pelvic pain is often multifactorial. Finding one diagnosis does not necessarily exclude another contributing condition.

rows: Painful periods, pain before or during menstruation
Endometriosis, adenomyosis, primary dysmenorrhoea
Heavy menstrual bleeding with a bulky, tender uterus
Adenomyosis or fibroids
Deep pain during sexual intercourse
Endometriosis, PID-related adhesions, pelvic floor dysfunction
Pain with bladder filling, relieved after urination
Bladder pain syndrome
Pain associated with defecation, bloating or altered bowel habits
IBS, endometriosis involving bowel, gastrointestinal disease
Pain after pelvic infection or surgery
Adhesions, chronic PID-related pain, nerve or abdominal wall pain
Pain worse with prolonged standing
Pelvic venous disorders or musculoskeletal causes
Persistent unilateral pain
Ovarian/adnexal pathology or other focal pelvic disease

blocks.text: These are clues, not diagnostic rules. For example, endometriosis may cause cyclical or continuous pain, and a patient can have normal imaging despite clinically significant disease.
Begin professionally:

“Good morning. My name is …, and I am a medical practitioner. I understand you have been experiencing pelvic pain for some time. I would like to ask you some questions about the pain, your menstrual and reproductive health, and how it affects your daily activities. Some questions may be personal, but they will help me understand what is happening. Is that okay?”

items.text: Confirm the patient's name and age.
Ensure privacy and confidentiality.
Ask permission before discussing sexual history.
Explain any intimate examination and obtain specific consent before proceeding.
Offer a chaperone for intimate examination according to local policy and patient preference.

blocks.text: Site
“Where exactly is the pain?”
Ask whether it is suprapubic, right or left iliac fossa, deep pelvic, vaginal, perineal or diffuse. Does it radiate to the back, groin, thighs or rectum?
Onset
“When did it start? Was it sudden or gradual?”
Establish the duration, first episode, progression, precipitating event and relationship to childbirth, miscarriage, pelvic infection or surgery.
Character
“How would you describe the pain?”
Cramping, aching, sharp, stabbing, burning, pressure-like or dragging. Ask whether there is a sensation of pelvic heaviness.
Radiation
“Does the pain spread anywhere else?”
Back pain may accompany adenomyosis or endometriosis; groin radiation may suggest urinary tract pathology, but neither is specific.
Associated symptoms
Ask about abnormal bleeding, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, dysuria, urinary frequency, constipation, diarrhoea, bloating, fever, weight loss and infertility.
Timing
“Is it there all the time, or does it come and go?”
Determine duration of episodes, frequency, nocturnal symptoms, menstrual relationship, postcoital pain and triggers such as standing, eating, urinating or defecating.
Exacerbating and relieving factors
Ask what worsens or relieves the pain: menstruation, intercourse, exercise, prolonged standing, bowel movements, urination, rest, analgesics or hormonal treatment.
Severity
“On a scale of 0 to 10, how severe is the pain?”
Ask how it affects walking, sleep, work, relationships, sexual activity and daily functioning. Compare the current pain with its worst level.
**C. Menstrual and gynaecological history**

items.text: Age at menarche.
First day of the last menstrual period (LMP).
Cycle regularity and usual cycle length.
Duration and amount of bleeding.
Heavy menstrual bleeding, flooding or clots.
Dysmenorrhoea and whether it has worsened over time.
Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Previous diagnoses of endometriosis, fibroids, adenomyosis or ovarian cysts.
Previous cervical screening and relevant results.
Menopausal status, if applicable.

blocks.text: Example of a significant finding: progressive dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and painful defecation around menstruation raise suspicion of endometriosis.
**D. Obstetric and fertility history**

items.text: Gravidity and parity.
Previous vaginal deliveries and caesarean sections.
Miscarriages, ectopic pregnancies and termination of pregnancy, where relevant.
Postpartum or post-procedure infection.
Difficulty conceiving and duration of attempts.
Previous fertility investigations or treatment.
Whether the patient desires pregnancy now or in the future.

blocks.text: Fertility wishes matter because some treatments for pelvic pain suppress ovulation or menstruation and are not compatible with trying to conceive.
**E. Sexual history**

items.text: Is the patient sexually active?
Is the pain superficial or deep during intercourse?
Is there postcoital bleeding?
Any vaginal discharge, odour or genital sores?
New or multiple sexual partners, if relevant.
Condom use and previous sexually transmitted infections.
Previous PID or treatment of a partner for an STI.

blocks.text: Do not assume that a patient with chronic pelvic pain has an STI, and do not interpret sexual history as a moral issue.
**F. Urinary and bowel history**
Urinary symptoms

items.text: Dysuria, frequency, urgency or nocturia.
Haematuria.
Pain as the bladder fills.
Whether voiding relieves the pain.
Recurrent UTIs or urinary stones.

blocks.text: Bowel symptoms

items.text: Constipation or diarrhoea.
Alternating bowel habits.
Bloating or excessive gas.
Pain on defecation, especially during menstruation.
Blood in stool, persistent change in bowel habits or unexplained weight loss.

blocks.text: Rectal bleeding during menstruation may raise suspicion of bowel endometriosis, but gastrointestinal causes must also be considered.
**G. Past history, medication and psychosocial impact**
Ask about previous abdominal or pelvic surgery, endometriosis, PID, urinary or bowel disease, trauma, current medications, allergies and response to previous treatments.

items.text: “How has the pain affected your work or studies?”
“Has it affected your sleep, mood or relationships?”
“What worries you most about the pain?”
“What treatments have you tried, and what helped?”
“What would you most like us to help you achieve?”

blocks.text: Chronic pain can coexist with anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance or past trauma. These should be explored sensitively, without implying that the pain is imaginary.
**H. Red flags — never miss these**
Although the presentation is chronic, a new acute change may signal an emergency.

items.text: Possible pregnancy, missed period or vaginal bleeding with pain.
Sudden severe pain, especially unilateral pain with nausea or vomiting.
Fever, rigors, marked pelvic tenderness or systemic illness.
Syncope, dizziness, hypotension or signs of internal bleeding.
Persistent postmenopausal bleeding.
Unexplained weight loss, early satiety, persistent abdominal distension or a pelvic mass.
Persistent haematuria, rectal bleeding or a significant change in bowel habits.
Severe pain with guarding or rebound tenderness.

blocks.text: If any of these are present, assess urgently rather than continuing a routine chronic-pain work-up.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm identity, explain the examination and obtain consent.
Ask about pain before touching the patient.
Offer a chaperone for intimate examination.
Provide privacy and appropriate draping.
Ask the patient to empty their bladder if appropriate.
Ensure adequate lighting and a comfortable position.
Explain that the patient can ask you to stop at any time.
General appearance, distress and mobility.
Temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate.
Pallor, dehydration and signs of systemic infection.
Weight or nutritional status where relevant.
Abdominal distension, scars or visible masses.

blocks.text: Example of normal reporting:
“The patient is comfortable at rest, afebrile and haemodynamically stable, with no obvious pallor or signs of systemic illness.”
Example of abnormal reporting:

“The patient appears uncomfortable and pale, with tachycardia and lower abdominal tenderness. I would assess urgently for anaemia, infection, pregnancy-related complications or intra-abdominal bleeding according to the clinical context.”
Perform inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation as appropriate.

items.text: Scars from previous surgery.
Abdominal distension.
Suprapubic or iliac fossa tenderness.
Guarding or rebound tenderness.
Palpable uterine or adnexal masses.
Hernias and abdominal wall tenderness.
Pain reproduced by abdominal wall muscle contraction, which may suggest an abdominal wall source.

rows: Suprapubic tenderness
Bladder pathology, pelvic inflammation or other pelvic disease
Enlarged, irregular lower abdominal mass
May suggest uterine fibroids
Lower abdominal guarding or rebound
Peritoneal irritation; urgent assessment needed
Focal abdominal wall tenderness that persists or increases when the abdominal muscles tense
May suggest abdominal wall pain
Distension with a palpable pelvic mass
Requires investigation for uterine, ovarian or other pelvic pathology

blocks.text: Do not diagnose a condition from one examination finding alone.
Perform only when indicated, with informed consent, appropriate training and a chaperone according to local policy.
External examination

items.text: Inspect the vulva and perineum for lesions, discharge, scarring or tenderness.
Look for signs of inflammation or other visible abnormalities.

blocks.text: Speculum examination

items.text: Assess vaginal walls and cervix.
Look for discharge, cervical lesions, contact bleeding or visible abnormalities.
Obtain swabs or cervical samples when indicated.

blocks.text: Bimanual examination

items.text: Assess cervical motion tenderness.
Assess uterine size, position, mobility and tenderness.
Assess adnexal tenderness or masses.
Look for restricted uterine mobility or nodularity where endometriosis is suspected.

blocks.text: A rectovaginal examination may occasionally help assess suspected deep endometriosis or posterior pelvic pathology, but only if indicated, appropriately consented to and performed by a suitably trained clinician.
Example 1 — suspected endometriosis

“There is reduced uterine mobility with posterior fornix tenderness and possible nodularity along the uterosacral ligaments. These findings raise suspicion of endometriosis, although further assessment is required.”
Example 2 — suspected adenomyosis
“The uterus feels enlarged and uniformly tender on bimanual examination. This may be consistent with adenomyosis in the appropriate clinical context.”
Example 3 — suspected fibroids
“The uterus is enlarged, irregular in contour and firm, suggesting uterine leiomyomas.”
Example 4 — suspected PID

“There is cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness, with vaginal discharge on speculum examination. PID is a clinical possibility and requires assessment for severity and alternative diagnoses.”
Example 5 — normal pelvic examination

“The vulva, vagina and cervix appear normal. There is no cervical motion tenderness, uterine enlargement or palpable adnexal mass. A normal examination does not exclude endometriosis, bladder pain syndrome or pelvic floor dysfunction.”

content_groups.group_title: E. Pelvic floor and musculoskeletal assessment

blocks.title: If appropriate and consented to, assess:

items.text: Pelvic floor muscle tone and tenderness.
Whether gentle palpation reproduces the patient's familiar pain.
Abdominal wall tenderness.
Hip, sacroiliac and lumbar spine movement.
Posture, gait and relevant neurological signs.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: if pain is reproduced by palpation of tight pelvic floor muscles, pelvic floor myalgia may be contributing. It can coexist with endometriosis or other pelvic pathology.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Differential diagnosis: how to reason through the case

rows: Endometriosis
Dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel/bladder symptoms, infertility
Transvaginal ultrasound; specialist ultrasound or MRI for deep disease; laparoscopy in selected cases
Adenomyosis
Heavy menstrual bleeding, dysmenorrhoea, uniformly enlarged tender uterus
Transvaginal ultrasound; MRI if needed
Fibroids
Heavy bleeding, pressure symptoms, enlarged irregular uterus
Pelvic ultrasound
Chronic PID or sequelae
Previous STI/PID, discharge, dyspareunia, cervical motion tenderness
STI testing, pregnancy test, ultrasound when indicated
Ovarian/adnexal pathology
Unilateral pain, fullness, mass or bloating
Pelvic ultrasound; further evaluation based on findings
IBS
Pain associated with defecation, bloating, altered stool frequency or form
Clinical assessment; targeted tests if alarm features are present
Bladder pain syndrome
Pain related to bladder filling, frequency and urgency
Urinalysis, urine culture and assessment for alternative urinary pathology
Pelvic floor dysfunction
Pain reproduced by muscle palpation, dyspareunia, urinary or bowel symptoms
Focused pelvic floor and musculoskeletal assessment

blocks.text: Remember to consider non-gynaecological disease and malignancy when the history, age, examination or red flags suggest them.
Investigations should be tailored to the history and examination rather than ordering every test for every patient.
1. Pregnancy test
Urine or serum β-hCG when pregnancy is biologically possible. A positive test with pelvic pain requires prompt assessment for ectopic pregnancy and other pregnancy complications.
2. Pelvic ultrasound

Transvaginal ultrasound, if acceptable and appropriate, usually provides good assessment of the uterus, endometrium and adnexa. Transabdominal ultrasound may be used where transvaginal scanning is unsuitable or declined.
3. Full blood count
Consider if heavy menstrual bleeding, pallor, fatigue, infection or other indications are present. Ferritin may help assess iron deficiency.
4. Urine and STI testing
Urinalysis and urine culture for urinary symptoms; nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea where indicated, with other infection tests according to risk and local guidance.

items.text: MRI pelvis: useful when ultrasound is inconclusive or mapping of deep endometriosis, adenomyosis or complex pelvic pathology is needed.

Laparoscopy: may be considered when endometriosis is suspected despite normal imaging, symptoms persist, or surgery is otherwise indicated. It is not required in every patient before initiating treatment.
Gastrointestinal investigations: based on bowel symptoms, age, examination and alarm features.
Cystoscopy or specialist urinary evaluation: in selected patients with persistent bladder symptoms or concerning findings.
Additional blood tests: inflammatory markers, renal function, endocrine tests or other tests depending on the suspected diagnosis.

blocks.text: CA-125 is not a diagnostic test for endometriosis and should not be ordered routinely for that purpose. It may be considered in specific contexts, such as assessment of a suspected ovarian malignancy, according to the relevant clinical pathway.

rows: Enlarged, irregular uterus with well-defined myometrial masses
Suggests fibroids
Globular uterus, heterogeneous myometrium or myometrial cysts
May suggest adenomyosis
Ovarian cyst with homogeneous low-level internal echoes
May suggest an endometrioma; correlate with the full scan and clinical findings
Deep infiltrating lesion or reduced organ mobility
May support deep endometriosis
Normal pelvic ultrasound
Does not exclude superficial endometriosis, pelvic floor dysfunction, IBS or bladder pain syndrome

blocks.text: The management goal is to reduce pain, improve function and quality of life, treat identifiable causes and support the patient's reproductive goals.

items.text: Explain that chronic pelvic pain is real and may have several contributing causes.
Agree on achievable treatment goals with the patient.
Treat identifiable underlying conditions.
Use appropriate pain relief, considering contraindications and adverse effects.
Offer pelvic floor physiotherapy where indicated.
Consider psychological support or pain services when pain is persistent or significantly affects daily life.
Arrange follow-up to review symptoms, treatment response and any new red flags.

blocks.text: Endometriosis

items.text: NSAIDs, if suitable, for pain relief.
Hormonal suppression, such as combined hormonal contraception or progestogen therapy, when appropriate and consistent with fertility goals.
Specialist-directed GnRH-based treatment for selected patients, with attention to adverse effects and any required add-back therapy.
Laparoscopic surgery for selected cases, including certain endometriomas or deep disease, or persistent symptoms despite appropriate treatment.
Fertility-focused counselling if pregnancy is desired.

blocks.text: Adenomyosis

items.text: NSAIDs or other suitable analgesia.
Hormonal treatment, including a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system in suitable patients.
Other hormonal options depending on bleeding, pain, contraindications and patient preference.
Specialist discussion of surgery for severe symptoms that persist despite medical treatment; hysterectomy is definitive for adenomyosis in patients who do not desire future pregnancy.

blocks.text: Uterine fibroids

items.text: Observe if asymptomatic or symptoms are mild.
Treat heavy menstrual bleeding and pain according to severity.
Consider medication, uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy or hysterectomy based on symptoms, fibroid characteristics and fertility wishes.

blocks.text: Pelvic floor dysfunction

items.text: Pelvic floor physiotherapy, often focusing on relaxation and muscle coordination when muscles are overactive or painful.
Education on pacing, posture and symptom triggers.
Selected psychological or pain-management interventions.
Avoid assuming that strengthening exercises such as repeated Kegels are appropriate for every patient; they may worsen pain in an overactive pelvic floor.

blocks.text: Bladder pain syndrome

items.text: Exclude infection and other relevant urinary pathology.
Individualised bladder and symptom management.
Consider pelvic floor physiotherapy and specialist referral when symptoms persist.

blocks.title: Refer to gynaecology or an appropriate specialist for:

items.text: Suspected endometriosis with persistent symptoms or possible deep disease.
A pelvic mass, suspicious imaging or concern for malignancy.
Persistent pain despite initial treatment.
Complex fertility-related decisions.
Suspected significant adhesions or complex pelvic pathology.
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring specialist assessment.

blocks.text: Urgent referral or emergency assessment is needed for acute deterioration, suspected ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, significant bleeding, sepsis or peritonism.

items.text: Physiotherapy for pelvic floor or musculoskeletal contributors.
Pain specialists for persistent, complex pain.
Psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy where acceptable to the patient.
Sleep support, pacing and graded return to activity.
Treatment of associated bowel or bladder disorders.
Sexual health and relationship support if pain affects intimacy.

blocks.text: These interventions complement medical care; they do not imply that the pain is psychological or unreal.
Scenario: A 30-year-old woman has experienced pelvic pain for nine months. Her ultrasound is normal, but endometriosis remains a possibility. Counsel her.
Step 1 — Acknowledge her symptoms

“I understand that you have been experiencing pelvic pain for several months, and that this may be affecting your daily life. I am sorry you have been going through this. I would like us to work together to understand the possible causes and find a treatment plan that helps.”
Step 2 — Explain the possible causes

“Pelvic pain can arise from several conditions, including endometriosis, painful or heavy periods, bladder or bowel problems, and pelvic floor muscle problems. Sometimes more than one condition contributes to the pain.”
Step 3 — Explain the normal ultrasound

“Your ultrasound has not shown an obvious abnormality, which is reassuring in some respects. However, some causes of pelvic pain, particularly superficial endometriosis, may not be visible on ultrasound. A normal scan does not mean that your pain is not real.”
Step 4 — Discuss the next steps

“I would like to review your symptoms, examine you with your permission, and consider whether further tests or specialist assessment are needed. Depending on the suspected cause, we may try pain relief, hormonal treatment, physiotherapy or other targeted treatments.”
Step 5 — Discuss fertility and preferences

“If you hope to become pregnant, please tell me, because that will influence our choice of treatment. Some hormonal treatments prevent pregnancy while you are taking them, so we should choose a plan that fits your goals.”
Step 6 — Safety-net
“If the pain suddenly becomes severe, you develop fainting, fever, heavy bleeding, persistent vomiting, or you might be pregnant and have pelvic pain, please seek urgent medical assessment.”
Step 7 — Check understanding
“What concerns you most about the pain? Is there anything you would like me to explain further?”

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the definition of chronic pelvic pain?
Persistent or recurrent pain perceived in the pelvic region, traditionally lasting at least six months. It may be cyclical or non-cyclical and may arise from several organ systems.
Q2. What are the common gynaecological causes?
Endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, chronic PID or its sequelae, ovarian/adnexal pathology and pelvic floor dysfunction.
Q3. What is the most important differential in a woman with chronic cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia?
Endometriosis is an important possibility, particularly when pain is progressive or associated with infertility or painful defecation.
Q4. Does a normal ultrasound exclude endometriosis?
No. Ultrasound can identify endometriomas and some forms of deep endometriosis, but superficial disease may not be visible.
Q5. When should you perform a pregnancy test?
Whenever pregnancy is biologically possible and pelvic pain is being assessed, particularly with missed periods or abnormal bleeding. Pregnancy-related emergencies must be excluded.
Q6. Is laparoscopy mandatory before treating suspected endometriosis?

No. Clinical assessment and imaging can guide initial treatment. Laparoscopy may be considered when imaging is negative but suspicion persists, treatment is unsuccessful or surgery is otherwise indicated.
Q7. Why is fertility history important?
It identifies possible subfertility associated with endometriosis or other pelvic disease and guides treatment choices. Some hormonal treatments are incompatible with actively trying to conceive.
Q8. What is the role of pelvic floor physiotherapy?
It can help patients with pelvic floor tenderness, muscle overactivity and associated musculoskeletal pain. It may be part of a broader multidisciplinary treatment plan.
Q9. What red flags require urgent assessment?
Possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding, sudden severe pain, haemodynamic instability, fever with significant pelvic tenderness, peritonism, or concerning findings suggesting malignancy.
Q10. How do you manage chronic pelvic pain when no clear cause is identified?

Reassess the differential, consider urinary, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal and neuropathic causes, provide appropriate symptom management, assess the impact on function and mental wellbeing, and arrange follow-up. Refer for specialist or multidisciplinary care if symptoms persist.

items.text: G — Gynaecological: endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID.
U — Urinary: bladder pain syndrome, UTI, stones.
P — Pelvic floor and musculoskeletal causes.
G — Gastrointestinal: IBS, constipation, bowel disease.
I — Interacting factors: neuropathic pain, sleep disturbance, psychological distress and other contributors to pain.

A — Associated symptoms: bleeding, discharge, bowel and bladder symptoms.
I — Impact: sleep, work, sexual function, fertility and mood.
N — Negative features and danger signs: pregnancy risk, fever, syncope, bleeding, weight loss.
T — Treat the underlying cause.
R — Relieve symptoms appropriately.
E — Explore fertility goals and patient preferences.
A — Address associated physical and psychosocial contributors.
T — Track progress, review and refer when needed.

Uterine fibroids only
Endometriosis
Uncomplicated cystitis
Primary amenorrhoea
2. A patient has persistent pelvic pain but a normal transvaginal ultrasound. What is the best interpretation?
Endometriosis is excluded
The pain must be psychological

CA-125 for every patient
Pregnancy test
Routine colonoscopy
Serum prolactin

Pelvic floor physiotherapy tailored to muscle overactivity

blocks.title: Before you finish the station, ensure that you have:

items.text: Characterised the pain using SOCRATES.
Established its relationship to menstruation, intercourse, urination and defecation.
Taken menstrual, obstetric, sexual and fertility histories.
Asked about urinary, bowel and psychosocial symptoms.
Screened for pregnancy and other red flags.
Explained and obtained consent for relevant examinations.
Suggested appropriate investigations.
Discussed cause-specific and multidisciplinary management.
Addressed fertility wishes, patient concerns and follow-up.
Provided clear safety-net advice.
